These tokens are only valid for read-only endpoints that are not restricted by a required scope. You can get a client access token by clicking "Generate Access Token" on the API Client management page. Genius uses the OAuth2 standard for making API calls on behalf of individual users. Requests are authenticated with an Access Token sent in an HTTP header (or as a request parameter if you must). All interaction with the API must be done over HTTPS. An example request would look like this: https://api.genius.com/oauth/authorize? client\_id=YOUR\_CLIENT\_ID& redirect\_uri=YOUR\_REDIRECT\_URI& scope=REQUESTED\_SCOPE& state=SOME\_STATE\_VALUE& response\_type=code Getting an Access Token Start by directing a user of your application to Genius's authentication page at https://api.genius.com/oauth/authorize with the following query parameters: client\_id: Your application's Client ID, as listed on the API Client management page redirect\_uri: The URI Genius will redirect the user to after they've authorized your application; it must be the same as the one set for the API client on the management page scope: The permissions your application is requesting as a space-separated list (see available scopes below) state: A value that will be returned with the code redirect for maintaining arbitrary state through the authorization process response\_type: Always "code" More About State One important use for this value is increased security—by including a unique, difficult to guess value (say, a hash of a user session value), potential attackers can be prevented from sending phony redirects to your app. On the authentication page the user can choose to allow your application to access Genius on their behalf. They'll be asked to sign in (or, if necessary, create an account) first. Then the user is redirected to https://YOUR\_REDIRECT\_URI/?code=CODE&state=SOME\_STATE\_VALUE. Your application can exchange the code query parameter from the redirect for an access token by making a POST request to https://api.genius.com/oauth/token with the following request body data: { "code": "CODE\_FROM\_REDIRECT", "client\_id": "YOUR\_CLIENT\_ID", "client\_secret": "YOUR\_CLIENT\_SECRET", "redirect\_uri": "YOUR\_REDIRECT\_URI", "response\_type": "code", "grant\_type": "authorization\_code" } code: The code query parameter from the redirect to your redirect\_uri client\_secret: Your application's Client Secret, as listed on the API Client management page grant\_type: Aways "authorization\_code" client\_id: As above redirect\_uri: As above response\_type: As above Most of these are the same values as used in the initial request. { "access\_token": "ACCESS\_TOKEN" } The response body will be an object with the token as the value for the access\_token key. It should thus be applicable to most design situations, bearing in mind that it caters for saturated conditions if necessary, in environments subjected to high rainfalls or periodic flooding.

The method, however, cannot be used directly if the proposed road is in deep cut or on a high fill, where the final formation level (selected subgrade or capping layer) is either below or above the currently exposed soil surface. In such cases, the cutting or embankment must be constructed to the formation height before testing of the support, using the DCP for the pavement design. However, in the case of embankments, the imported material to be used for the embankment can be tested using the DCP in the laboratory to understand its properties: this material will provide the final construction level on which the pavement can then be designed using the DCP.

Similarly, in soil cut areas, the final “subgrade” level can be tested using the DCP after excavation. However, if the cut is in rock, testing with the DCP would not give any meaningful results.

Although testing of very stony materials will often give a DCP result, this can be considered unreliable due to the number of additional blows that may be necessary to break or “by-pass” larger materials.

2.3.1 Previous Studies on L2 Motivational Self-System
As an important factor affecting learning effectiveness, learners' motivation has received the attention of many researchers, who have explored the nature of motivation from various research perspectives （Wang Xiaomin & Zhang Wenzhong, 2005). Foreign language motivation has gone through four major developmental stages: 1. the psychosocial period (1959-1990); 2. the cognitive context period (1990s); 3. the process-oriented period (2000-2005); and 4. the social dynamic period (now) (Jin Haiyun, 2013). Dörnyei's L2MSS theory is the latest achievement in this period. Research at home and abroad on L2 motivational self-system can be divided into confirmatory studies of L2 motivational self-system and correlation studies of L2 motivational self-system with other variables.
2.3.1.1 Confirmatory studies of L2 motivational self-system at home and abroad
The L2MSS has got strong reactions in the academic circles since its introduction. Dörnyei and Csizer et al. (2006) conducted a large-scale empirical study in Hungary with more than 13,000 students and concluded that the ideal L2 self and the ought-to L2 self play an important role in language learning. Since this famous study, researchers have conducted a great number of empirical studies in different countries such as Hungary (Csizer & Kormos, 2009), Japan (Ryan, 2009), Iran, and China (Taguchi, Magid & Papi, 2009) to verify the validity and operationalization of L2MSS.
Csizer and Kormos (2009) took a questionnaire to investigate the similarities and differences in the motivation of Hungarian learners at different levels, and also compared the relationship between the ideal L2 self and the ought-to L2 self of the L2MSS and traditional motivation. The study verified the validity of L2MSS in the Hungarian context, and they found that the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self, and the L2 learning experience are independent motivational factors. Ryan (2009) conducted an empirical study of 2397 college and high school English learners from a variety of schools and found that the ideal L2 self was very highly correlated with traditional integrative motivation, but Dörnyei's ideal L2 self was more effective than Gardner's integrative motivation in explaining motivated behavior of learners. Taguchi, Magid, and Papi (2009) carried out a large empirical study of nearly 5,000 students from three Asian countries (China, Japan, and Iran), including middle school students, college students majoring in English and non-English, and adult language learners. Through correlation analysis and structural equation modeling, this study also confirmed the validity of the three components of L2MSS and validated the theory in these three Asian countries. In China, Liu, Fengge (2012) found that the ideal L2 self is more relevant to second language motivation than the traditional integrative motivation for Chinese English learners, which is similar with the conclusion of Dörnyei and Ryan.
And then she carried out a study to test the validity of the L2MSS in a Chinese language learning context with 956 English learners of five different English levels (Elementary and middle school students, English major undergraduates, non-English major undergraduates, English major postgraduates, non-English major postgraduates) (2015). The results showed that the L2MSS is applicable to investigate the motivation of all kinds of Chinese learners who learn English as a foreign language, and the ideal L2 self is more powerful than the integrative motivation in explaining learners motivation. Since then, there has been a growing body of research on L2MSS in China.
These studies validated Dörnyei's "L2MSS" and showed that the theory can be used in different language learning contexts, which also provided insight for the implementation of this study.

A 75-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus and peripheral vascular disease is 
admitted with a gangrenous ulcer of the plantar aspect of her left foot. A surgical consultation results in a recommendation for a below-the-knee amputation, but the patient declines the procedure on the grounds that she has lived long enough and wants 
to die with her body intact. Her internist, who has known her for 15 years, is concerned that she has been increasingly confused over the past year and now appears to 
be depressed. How should her physician determine whether her decision is a competent one?
The Cl inic a l Problem
Physicians are required by law and medical ethics to obtain the informed consent of 
their patients before initiating treatment.1 Valid informed consent is premised on the 
disclosure of appropriate information to a competent patient who is permitted to make 
a voluntary choice. When patients lack the competence to make a decision about treatment, substitute decision makers must be sought. Hence, the determination of whether patients are competent is critical in striking a proper balance between respecting 
the autonomy of patients who are capable of making informed decisions and protecting those with cognitive impairment.
Although incompetence denotes a legal status that in principle should be determined by a court, resorting to judicial review in every case of suspected impairment 
of capacity would probably bring both the medical and legal systems to a halt. (The 
terms “competence” and “capacity” are used interchangeably in this article, since the 
oft-cited distinctions between them — competence is said to refer to legal judgments, 
and capacity to clinical ones — are not consistently reflected in either legal or medical 
usage.) Thus, in most situations there is good reason to continue the traditional practice of having physicians determine patients’ capacity and decide when to seek substituted consent.2 Indeed, statutes regarding advance directives for medical treatment 
generally recognize a medical determination of incapacity as the trigger for activating 
these directives.3 In addition, since consent obtained from an incompetent patient 
is invalid, physicians who do not obtain a substituted decision may be subject to 
claims of having treated the person without informed consent.1 Physicians must therefore be aware that their patients may have impaired decision-making capacities, and 
they must be skilled at evaluating that possibility.
Patients whose competence is impaired are commonly found in medical and surgical inpatient units, and less frequently in outpatient clinics. Between 3 and 25% of 
requests for psychiatric consultation in hospital settings involve questions about patients’ competence to make treatment-related decisions.4,5 In many other cases, impaired decision making in hospitalized patients may go undetected,6-9 even when

Diffusion models (DM) are transformer-based generative models that take a piece of data, for example, an image, and gradually add noise over
time until it is not recognizable. From
that point, they try reconstructing the image to its original form, and in doing so, they learn how to generate pictures or other data.
The issue with DMs is that the powerful ones often consume hundreds of GPU days, and inference is quite expensive due to sequential
evaluations. To enable DM training on limited computational resources without compromising their quality as well as flexibility, DMs are applied in
the latent space of powerful pre-trained autoencoders.
Training a diffusion model on such a representation makes it possible to achieve an optimal point between complexity reduction and detail
preservation, significantly improving visual fidelity. Introducing a cross-attention layer to the model architecture turns the diffusion model into a
powerful and flexible generator for generally conditioned inputs such as text and bounding boxes, enabling high-resolution convolution-based
synthesis.

For the course you will build the content for a powerpoint slide and then the transcript for that slide, one slide after another. This is the information to teach:

Introduction
Investigations for patients with clinical stage I/II melanoma are undertaken to determine prognosis and identify early metastatic disease in the regional lymph nodes (stage III) or distant organs (stage IV). Investigations such as diagnostic imaging, ultrasonography, skin examination and blood tests are conducted for initial staging and also as a part of a follow-up program after definitive surgical treatment. Sentinel node biopsy, is also undertaken for staging and prognostic purposes, however for discussion of this procedure we refer readers to the specific guideline for use of sentinel node biopsy in staging cutaneous melanoma.

The main purpose of follow-up is to detect recurrences early so that early treatment can be undertaken. This assumes that earlier treatment is likely to result in improvements in regional disease control, quality of life and survival. Therefore, follow-up should be mainly prognosis-oriented but should also include the detection of new invasive melanomas. The reported incidence of new primaries ranges from >0.5% to 5% annually dependent on risk features.[1][2] A second invasive melanoma is most commonly thinner than the initial primary melanoma and has a more favourable prognosis that does not adversely affect survival.[3] The rate of occurrence of a subsequent in-situ melanoma is about four times higher than the risk of a subsequent invasive melanoma[4], but most series do not recommend follow-up for in-situ melanomas.[5]

After systematic review of the literature (2012-2016) including previous melanoma guidelines, we considered the evidence base for the use of diagnostic tests for initial staging and follow-up. NHMRC levels of evidence (I-IV) were assigned to each evidence summary statement and recommendations were formed and graded with regard to consistency, clinical impact, generalisability, and applicability for the Australian context. Investigations reviewed in this chapter include chest x-ray, computed tomography (CT) imaging, positron emission tomography (PET)/CT imaging, ultrasonography, and S 100B, MIA, LDH blood tests. Additional experimental investigations identified through our systematic search, are discussed in the section for further research.

The evidence below is a summary of the key findings of test accuracy and clinical usefulness for each diagnostic investigation. We report sensitivity and specificity, positive and negative predictive values where available as the main test performance characteristics for the index test compared to the referent (gold) standard. For follow-up, the proportion resulting in a change in management and/or a change in morbidity and mortality are presented if known. The evidence and recommendations for optimal follow-up settings, duration and frequency are discussed in a separate chapter (see following section)

Nearly all studies for initial staging and follow-up were retrospective in design, at high risk of bias and of NHMRC level III or IV (lower quality) evidence. Several follow-up studies grouped stage II and III patients making ascertainment of benefits or harms from diagnostic investigations difficult. All included results are for stage I/II patients unless otherwise indicated.

Investigations for stage I and stage II melanoma in patients with a negative sentinel node
Imaging
Chest x-ray (CXR) for initial staging
There was only one new study published since 2012. This retrospective study investigated use of pre-operative imaging for 546 clinically node negative cutaneous melanoma patients undergoing sentinel lymph node biopsy. In total 409/546 (75%) had an imaging study: 383 (70%)had a CXR, 53 had CT scans (10%; included 43 CT chest, 34 CT abdomen/pelvis, 2 CT head, 4 CT neck), 25 PET scans (5%), 20 MRI scans (4%; included 18 head MRI, 1 extremity MRI and 1 spine MRI), and 2 people had extremity X-rays (0.4%).[6] Of the 383 people who had CXR, three had positive findings, all of which were false positives (all had negative chest CT scans; false positive rate 0.8%, true positive rate 0%). The 380 negative results were all true negatives. Pre-operative imaging for detection of metastases was not recommended.

Given the limited number of new studies on CXR, a review of the recommendations from previous guidelines was warranted.[3] Among 17 studies, CXR detected stage IV metastatic disease in a few patients; however the test results did not change clinical management, and did not improve overall survival. CXR had a false positive rate of between 2-71%, and a true positive rate of 0%.[7] The evidence base for guidance on use of CXR consisted of small observational studies, with no RCTs, with medium to high risk of bias (NHMRC level of evidence III-2 to IV).

Chest x-ray (CXR) during follow-up
The use of routine chest X-ray exams for the detection of small pulmonary metastases has been investigated. However, false-positive and false-negative findings are frequent. The sensitivity of chest X-ray is poor with reports varying from 7.7% to 48%. A large study of 1969 patients with stage I-III melanoma undergoing routine follow up found that only 10/204 relapses were discovered by chest X-ray: the majority (7/10) of which were observed in patients with stage III disease.[8] A large prospective study of 1 235 patients found that only 0.9% of chest X-rays identified pulmonary metastases, less than 10% of which were amenable to resection, with a false positive rate of 3.1%.[9] A cost-effectiveness analysis using data from the Roswell Park Cancer Institute and the National Cancer Institute’s Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program found that the cost of CXR screening per quality-adjusted life year was $165,000, respectively, in 1996 US dollars.[10] Based on these findings, the investigators suggested reducing the frequency of screening CXR.

Computed tomography (CT) imaging for initial staging
One retrospective study of 172 patients with clinically stage IIB or IIC melanoma evaluated the use of CT of the head, chest, abdomen and pelvis for initial staging.[11] In total 75 patients had 104 CT scans for initial staging, with 8 positive results, of which 6 were false positives and two true positives in one patient with metastatic disease, and one patient with a secondary non-melanoma cancer.

Computed tomography (CT) imaging during follow-up
No new studies of CT surveillance of asymptomatic patients treated for stage I/II melanoma were identified. Existing guidelines and prior studies report little benefit in terms of early detection of metastatic disease, a change in clinical management, improved survival, or cost-effectiveness.[12][13]

Positron emission tomography (PET) or computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging for initial staging
One retrospective study among 106 patients with head and neck primary melanoma, clinically negative nodal disease and negative CT, evaluated the use of FDG-PET for initial staging.[14] In total 47 patients had FDG-PET, with 10 positive results, of which 8 were false positives and two true positives in patients with secondary non-melanoma cancers. Of the 37 patients with a negative FDG-PET, 33 results were true negatives and four were false negatives in patients with occult nodal disease. FDG-PET was found to have no clinical utility in this patient population.[14]

Five new studies using PET/CT were identified, including one systematic review[15], two primary studies assessing detection of nodal disease[16][17] and four assessing detection of distant metastases.[15][17][18][19] In one retrospective study of 149 patients undergoing pre-operative PET/CT imaging for clinically stage I/II melanoma of at least 1 mm thickness, 41 had positive findings, 35 were false positives and 6 were true positives (metastatic involvement of lymph node confirmed histologically; false positive rate 85%, true positive rate 15%).[18] There was no clinical utility associated with PET/CT above and beyond SNB: false positives led to unnecessary invasive procedures, and true positives yielded no further information to the SNB. The authors concluded pre-operative PET/CT was of limited benefit in staging clinical stage I/II patients.[18] Another study compared sensitivity and specificity of PET/CT versus high resolution ultrasound for the identification of metastatic involvement of sentinel lymph node.[16] The sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV of PET/CT were 0%, 100% (95%CI 91.6–100.0), 0% and 71.1% (95% CI 58.6–81.2) respectively. The authors concluded high resolution ultrasound was better value than PET/CT in preoperative identification of positive SLNs. A second retrospective study of 77 clinically stage I/II melanoma patients aimed to identify a threshold thickness for the primary melanoma, above which PET/CT might be useful.[19] All but 1 of the 11 patients with positive PET/CT findings had melanomas ≥5mm (only 5 positive PET/CT results were confirmed true positives histologically: 4 lymph node metastases, 1 distant metastasis). Four of the 11 patients with positive PET/CT (36%), and 5 of 66 patients with negative PET/CT (8%), died from melanoma. It was unclear whether the PET/CT results influenced clinical management.[19]

In general, against a histopathology reference standard PET/CT generally had moderate to low sensitivity and higher specificity. High false positive rates including detection of benign lesions and other cancers led to additional investigations including invasive procedures.[15][18] Some melanoma metastases were missed on PET/CT being detected clinically within 6 months of the index scan,[17] or detected with SNB.[14]

Positron emission tomography (PET) or computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging during follow up
A recent systematic review by Danielson et al[20] of 7 studies was undertaken to assess the diagnostic value of PET as a tool for surveillance in the regular follow-up program of asymptomatic cutaneous malignant melanoma patients. The majority of the 739 patients in the studies were stage IIB and III. The authors concluded that the mean sensitivity of PET was 96% (95% CI: 92-98) and the specificity was 92% (95% CI: 87-95). Overall, PET has a high diagnostic value. However, there were no data available to demonstrate better survival outcomes for patients as a result of routine PET surveillance.[20]

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for initial staging
The retrospective study of 546 patients discussed above under CXR also included MRI scans used for initial staging in 20 patients (4%; included 18 head MRI, 1 extremity MRI and 1 spine MRI).[6] The one positive MRI test result was a false positive in a patient with a benign thyroid nodule. The 19 negative results were all true negatives.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for during follow-up
Cerebral metastases are more readily detected by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) than by CT or FDG-PET/CT.[21], however no new studies published since 2012 of MRI follow-up of stage I/II patients were identified.

 - name: Run Functional Verification Test

This is a GitHub Actions workflow that runs a series of tests on a pull request to the `master` branch with tags starting with `v`. The workflow checks out the code, sets up the environment and tools, lints the YAML files, checks the code formatting, runs unit tests, and finally runs a functional verification test (FVT). The FVT suite creates a Docker environment to run tests and archives the code coverage results.

 - name: Setup tools used by WaaS

 with:
 version: 'waas/v1alpha4'
 - name: Auth GCP

 - name: Setup GCP CLI
 uses: google-github-actions/setup-gcloud@v0
 with:

 - name: Decrypt secrets to get docker login credentials
 id: decrypt\_docker\_secrets
 uses: metro-digital/sops-decrypt@v0.x
 with:
 version: ${{ env.SOPS\_VERSION }}
 file: 'waas-config/base/application.secrets.yaml'
 gpg\_key: ${{ secrets.GPG\_KEY }}
 output\_type: json
 - name: Login to container registry
 run: |
 set +e
 set -o pipefail
 username=$(echo $connection\_string | cut -d: -f2 | cut -d/ -f3)
 password=$(echo $connection\_string | cut -d@ -f1 | cut -d: -f3)
 hostname=$(echo $connection\_string | cut -d@ -f2 | cut -d/ -f1)
 echo "Login to docker registry $hostname"
 echo -n "$password" | docker login "$hostname" -u "$username" --password-stdin
 if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
 echo "::error ::WaaS: build: login to docker registry failed"
 exit 10
 fi
 env:
 connection\_string: ${{ fromJson(steps.decrypt\_docker\_secrets.outputs.data).DRP\_PF\_DOCKER\_1 }}
 - name: Check if docker image exist in container registry
 id: check\_for\_existing\_docker\_image
 run: |
 set +e
 set -o pipefail
 image=$(skaffold --default-repo=registry.metroscales.io/inventory build -q --dry-run | jq -r ".builds[0].tag")
 if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
 echo "::error ::WaaS: build: check for docker image: skaffold build failed"
 exit 15
 fi
 imageExist=$(docker manifest inspect $image > /dev/null && echo "true" || echo "false")
 echo "needed=${imageExist}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 - name: Build & push artifact
 id: build\_and\_push\_training\_artifact
 run: |
 set +e
 set -o pipefail
 echo "Building archive and push it into artifactory"
 cd gcp/scripts
 sh ./artifactory\_package.sh ${{ github.run\_number }}
 if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
 echo "::error ::WaaS: build: build\_and\_push\_training\_artifact: Training artifact build Failed"
 exit 15
 fi
 echo "true"
 - name: Build & push image to container registry (if needed)
 id: build\_and\_push\_docker\_image
 if: steps.check\_for\_existing\_docker\_image.outputs.needed == 'false'
 run: |
 set +e
 set -o pipefail
 skaffold --default-repo=registry.metroscales.io/inventory build -p push
 if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
 echo "::error ::WaaS: build: skaffold build and push failed"
 exit 20
 fi

 - name: Start port forwarding

 ps aux | grep -i kubectl
 echo Started port forwarding
 - name: Run a test curl to the liveliness probe
 run: |
 curl -fail --location http://localhost:8080/.well-known/live
 echo Service up and running
 - name: Get a token
 id: get-access-token
 run: |
 secret\_name=`kubectl get secrets -l repository.name=ml-markdown-optimizer --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp -o json | jq -r .items[-1].metadata.name`
 echo "Current deployment using secret ${secret\_name}"

 idam\_client\_id=`kubectl get secrets/${secret\_name} --template={{.data.IDAM\_CLIENT\_ID}} | base64 -d`
 idam\_client\_secret=`kubectl get secrets/${secret\_name} --template={{.data.IDAM\_CLIENT\_SECRET}} | base64 -d`
 idam\_token\_uri=`kubectl get secrets/${secret\_name} --template={{.data.IDAM\_TOKEN\_URI}} | base64 -d`
 idam\_grant\_type="client\_credentials"
 idam\_scope="openid"
 idam\_realm\_id="MSTORE\_RL"

 access\_token=`curl --silent --show-error --location --location --request POST ${idam\_token\_uri} --header "Accept: application/json" --header "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" --data-urlencode "client\_id=${idam\_client\_id}" --data-urlencode "client\_secret=${idam\_client\_secret}" --data-urlencode "grant\_type=${idam\_grant\_type}" --data-urlencode "scope=${idam\_scope}" --data-urlencode "realm\_id=${idam\_realm\_id}" | jq -r .access\_token`
 echo "::add-mask::${access\_token}"
 echo "access\_token=${access\_token}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 echo "::add-mask::${idam\_client\_id}"
 echo "idam\_client\_id=${idam\_client\_id}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 echo "::add-mask::${idam\_client\_secret}"
 echo "idam\_client\_secret=${idam\_client\_secret}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 echo "::add-mask::${idam\_token\_uri}"
 echo "idam\_token\_uri=${idam\_token\_uri}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 echo "::add-mask::${idam\_grant\_type}"
 echo "idam\_grant\_type=${idam\_grant\_type}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 echo "::add-mask::${idam\_scope}"
 echo "idam\_scope=${idam\_scope}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 echo "::add-mask::${idam\_realm\_id}"
 echo "idam\_realm\_id=${idam\_realm\_id}" >> $GITHUB\_OUTPUT
 - name: Set up python 3.9
 uses: actions/setup-python@v4
 with:
 python-version: 3.9
 architecture: 'x64'
 - name: Run FVT tests

Prompt engineering is a concept in artificial intelligence that involves designing prompts or input text to generate specific output text using machine learning algorithms. In other words, it is the process of instructing an AI to do a task by telling the AI a set of instructions or prompting it with a question or statement [[3](https://businessolution.org/prompt-engineering/)].

The description of the task is embedded in the input, e.g., as a question instead of it being implicitly given. By carefully selecting and structuring the input data, it is possible to build models that can handle a wide range of inputs and perform well even in the presence of noise [[7](https://www.c-sharpcorner.com/article/what-is-prompt-engineering-and-why-it-might-be-your-next-career-path/)]. Prompt engineering typically works by converting one or more tasks to a prompt-based dataset and training a language model with what has been called "prompt-based learning" or just "prompt learning" [[1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prompt_engineering)].

Prompt engineering is a very recent but rapidly growing discipline that has the goal of designing the optimal prompt given a generative model and a goal. It is growing so quickly that it might be the career of the future, with a viral job posting for a role with a salary range of $250k-$335k [[2](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/prompt-engineering-101-introduction-resources-amatriain)][[10](https://medium.com/sopmac-ai/what-does-a-prompt-engineer-do-f00c6f2ad1ab)].

Prompts can vary in complexity from a phrase to a question to multiple paragraphs worth of text. Effective prompt engineering involves discovering inputs that yield desirable or useful results, as the quality of the inputs determines the quality of the outputs in prompt engineering. Designing effective prompts increases the likelihood that the model will return a response that is both favorable and contextual [[9](https://fourweekmba.com/prompt-engineering/)].

Overall, prompt engineering serves as a starting point for teaching the AI model to develop outputs that are appropriate to a given task. It is a critical aspect of natural language processing and AI development and can be used to create more accurate and efficient models that can perform well in real-world scenarios [[5](https://www.unite.ai/what-is-prompt-engineering-in-ai-why-it-matters/)][[6](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/what-prompt-engineering-luthando-mkhwanazi)][[8](https://technostyle.substack.com/p/the-ultimate-guide-to-prompt-engineering)].

How Navigation Works
A route transition is initiated using or calling router.push().
The router updates the URL in the browser’s address bar.
The router avoids unnecessary work by re-using segments that haven't changed (e.g. shared layouts) from the client-side cache. This is also referred to as partial rendering.
If the conditions of soft navigation are met, the router fetches the new segment from the cache rather than the server. If not, the router performs a hard navigation and fetches the Server Component payload from the server.
If created, loading UI is shown from the server while the payload is being fetched.
The router uses the cached or fresh payload to render the new segments on the client.
Client-side Caching of Rendered Server Components
Good to know: This client-side cache is different from the server-side Next.js HTTP cache.

The new router has an in-memory client-side cache that stores the rendered result of Server Components (payload). The cache is split by route segments which allows invalidation at any level and ensures consistency across concurrent renders.

As users navigate around the app, the router will store the payload of previously fetched segments and prefetched segments in the cache.

This means, for certain cases, the router can re-use the cache instead of making a new request to the server. This improves performance by avoiding re-fetching data and re-rendering components unnecessarily.

Invalidating the Cache
The cache can be invalidated using router.refresh(). For more information, see the API reference. In the future, mutations will automatically invalidate the cache.

Prefetching
Prefetching is a way to preload a route in the background before it's visited. The rendered result of prefetched routes is added to the router's client-side cache. This makes navigating to a prefetched route near-instant.

By default, routes are prefetched as they become visible in the viewport when using the component. This can happen when the page first loads or through scrolling. Routes can also be programmatically prefetched using the prefetch method of the useRouter() hook.

Static and Dynamic Routes:

If the route is static, all the Server Component payloads for the route segments will be prefetched.
If the route is dynamic, the payload from the first shared layout down until the first loading.js file is prefetched. This reduces the cost of prefetching the whole route dynamically and allows instant loading states for dynamic routes.
Good to know:

Prefetching is only enabled in production.
Prefetching can be disabled by passing prefetch={false} to .
Hard Navigation
On navigation, the cache is invalidated and the server refetches data and re-renders the changed segments.

Soft Navigation
On navigation, the cache for changed segments is reused (if it exists), and no new requests are made to the server for data.

Conditions for Soft Navigation
On navigation, Next.js will use soft navigation if the route you are navigating to has been prefetched, and either doesn't include dynamic segments or has the same dynamic parameters as the current route.

For example, consider the following route that includes a dynamic [team] segment: /dashboard/[team]/\*. The cached segments below /dashboard/[team]/\* will only be invalidated when the [team] parameter changes.

Navigating from /dashboard/team-red/\* to /dashboard/team-red/\* will be a soft navigation.
Navigating from /dashboard/team-red/\* to /dashboard/team-blue/\* will be a hard navigation.
Back/Forward Navigation
Back and forward navigation (popstate event) has a soft navigation behavior. This means, the client-side cache is re-used and navigation is near-instant.

Focus and Scroll Management
By default, Next.js will set focus and scroll into view the segment that's changed on navigation. The importance of this accessibility and usability feature will be more apparent when advanced routing patterns are implemented.

1.1 Cognitive disorders are an important medical and social problem
a. Definition of cognitive disorders
Cognitive disorders, also referred to as neurocognitive disorders, are a category of mental health disorders that primarily affect cognitive abilities, including learning, memory, perception, and problem-solving. These disorders encompass a wide range of impairments, from mild to severe, and can result from various causes such as genetics, traumatic brain injury, infections, and neurodegenerative diseases (DSM-5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Cognitive disorders can manifest in various ways, such as difficulties in paying attention, processing information, planning, organizing, and making decisions.
b. Types of cognitive disorders and their etiology
Cognitive disorders can be broadly classified into the following categories, with a specific emphasis on memory impairment:
c. Emphasis on memory impairment:
Mild and major neurocognitive disorders (previously known as dementia): These disorders are characterized by a decline in cognitive function, including memory loss, and can be caused by various conditions such as Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and frontotemporal dementia (DSM-5; American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Alzheimer's disease, the most common cause of dementia, is characterized by the progressive accumulation of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brain, leading to neuronal death and brain atrophy (Querfurth & LaFerla, 2010). The exact cause of Alzheimer's disease is still unknown, but a combination of genetic, environmental, and lifestyle factors is believed to contribute to its development (Ballard et al., 2011). Vascular dementia, the second most common type, results from reduced blood flow to the brain due to conditions such as stroke or small vessel disease (O'Brien & Thomas, 2015). Vascular dementia is often associated with cerebrovascular risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, and smoking (Gorelick et al., 2011). Other less common forms of dementia include Lewy body dementia, which is characterized by abnormal protein deposits called Lewy bodies in the brain (McKeith et al., 2005), and frontotemporal dementia, which is caused by the degeneration of the frontal and temporal lobes of the brain (Rascovsky et al., 2011).
Amnestic disorders: These disorders primarily affect memory, including anterograde and retrograde amnesia, and can result from various causes such as brain injury, substance abuse, and certain medications (Kopelman, 2002). Anterograde amnesia refers to the inability to form new memories, while retrograde amnesia involves the inability to recall previously learned information (Tulving & Craik, 2000). Anterograde amnesia is commonly associated with damage to the hippocampus, a brain region critical for memory formation, while retrograde amnesia is often related to damage to the medial temporal lobe or diencephalic structures (Squire & Zola-Morgan, 1991). Both types of amnesia can result from a variety of causes, including traumatic brain injury, hypoxia, encephalitis, and chronic alcohol abuse (Kopelman, 2002).
In addition to memory impairment, cognitive disorders can involve other cognitive domains, such as attention, executive function, language, and visuospatial abilities. Some examples of other cognitive disorders include delirium, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and specific learning disorders (e.g., dyslexia, dyscalculia).
d. Prevalence of cognitive disorders
Cognitive disorders, particularly those affecting memory, are becoming increasingly prevalent as the global population ages. The World Health Organization
(2017) estimates that around 50 million people worldwide have dementia, with nearly 10 million new cases occurring each year. Alzheimer's disease accounts for 60-70% of these cases (World Health Organization, 2017). The prevalence of dementia is expected to increase significantly in the coming decades, with the number of affected individuals projected to reach 82 million by 2030 and 152 million by 2050 (Prince et al., 2015). This trend is primarily driven by population aging, as the risk of developing dementia increases with age (Ferri et al., 2005).
The prevalence of amnestic disorders is more challenging to estimate due to the varying etiology and the overlap with other cognitive disorders. However, these disorders are not uncommon, particularly in cases of traumatic brain injury or substance abuse (Kopelman, 2002).
e. Impact of cognitive disorders on individuals
Cognitive disorders can significantly impact an individual's quality of life, leading to difficulties in daily functioning, communication, and self-care. These disorders often result in emotional distress, increased dependence on caregivers, and reduced social engagement (Livingston et al., 2017). For example, individuals with Alzheimer's disease may experience a decline in their ability to perform daily activities such as dressing, eating, and managing finances (Alzheimer's Association, 2021). Furthermore, cognitive disorders can lead to feelings of frustration, isolation, and depression, as individuals struggle to cope with their changing abilities and the potential stigma associated with their condition (Cahill et al., 2015).
Cognitive disorders can also affect an individual's relationships with family and friends, as they may require increased support and understanding from their loved ones. Caregivers often face significant challenges in adapting to their new roles, balancing the needs of the affected individual with their own personal and professional responsibilities (Schulz & Sherwood, 2008).
f. Impact of cognitive disorders on society
Cognitive disorders, particularly those involving memory impairment, have considerable societal implications. The increasing prevalence of these disorders, due in part to an aging population, places a significant burden on healthcare systems and social support services. The need for long-term care, specialized healthcare services, and caregiver support is projected to grow in the coming years (Prince et al., 2015). In addition, cognitive disorders can strain relationships within families and communities, as individuals may require increased assistance from family members and friends. This can lead to caregiver burnout, financial strain, and increased demands on social services (Schulz & Sherwood, 2008).
The societal impact of cognitive disorders is further exacerbated by the stigma associated with these conditions. Misconceptions about cognitive disorders, such as the belief that they are a normal part of aging or that they are untreatable, can lead to delayed diagnosis, inadequate support, and social isolation for affected individuals and their families (Alzheimer's Disease International, 2012).
g. Economic consequences of cognitive disorders
The economic impact of cognitive disorders is substantial. In 2015, the global cost of dementia alone was estimated at $818 billion, with projections indicating that this figure could reach $2 trillion by 2030 (Wimo et al., 2017). These costs include direct medical expenses, social care costs, and the indirect costs associated with lost productivity and caregiver burden.
Direct medical costs for individuals with cognitive disorders include expenses related to diagnostic services, hospitalizations, medications, and other healthcare services. Social care costs include the provision of home care services, adult day care, and residential care facilities. Indirect costs encompass the lost productivity of both the affected individuals and their caregivers, as well as the emotional and physical toll caregiving can take on family members (Wimo et al., 2017).
h. Importance of early detection and intervention
Early detection and intervention in cognitive disorders, particularly those involving memory impairment, are crucial in mitigating their impact on individuals and society. Timely diagnosis allows for better planning, access to appropriate healthcare services, and the implementation of interventions that may slow cognitive decline or improve quality of life (Dubois et al., 2016). For example, pharmacological treatments such as cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine have been shown to provide modest symptomatic benefits in some individuals with Alzheimer's disease (Birks, 2006; McShane et al., 2006). Non-pharmacological interventions, such as cognitive stimulation, physical exercise, and social engagement, may also help maintain cognitive function and improve well-being in individuals with mild to moderate cognitive impairment (Bahar-Fuchs et al., 2013; Groot et al., 2016).
In addition to pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions, early detection and intervention can also facilitate better communication and decision-making between affected individuals, their families, and healthcare providers. This may involve discussions about care preferences, legal and financial planning, and the potential need for future support services (Boustani et al., 2016).
i. The role of risk factor modification and prevention
Given the substantial impact of cognitive disorders on individuals, families, and society, there is growing interest in identifying modifiable risk factors and implementing preventive strategies. Research has suggested that several lifestyle factors may contribute to the risk of developing cognitive disorders, including physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, and social isolation (Livingston et al., 2020). Addressing these risk factors through public health initiatives, such as promoting regular physical activity, healthy eating, smoking cessation, and social engagement, may help reduce the incidence of cognitive disorders and improve overall cognitive health (Livingston et al., 2020).
Moreover, the management of vascular risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia, has also been identified as a key strategy for preventing cognitive decline and dementia (Gorelick et al., 2011). For example, the control of blood pressure in midlife has been associated with a reduced risk of late-life dementia (Launer et al., 2000). Similarly, interventions targeting glycemic control in individuals with diabetes may help prevent cognitive decline and dementia (Biessels et al., 2006).
In summary, cognitive disorders, particularly those affecting memory, represent a significant medical and social problem. These disorders impact individuals' quality of life, strain healthcare systems and social support services, and have substantial economic consequences. Early detection and intervention, as well as the modification of lifestyle and vascular risk factors, are crucial in addressing the growing challenge of cognitive disorders in our aging society.
j. The role of nutrition and dietary mineral composition in cognitive health
Emerging evidence suggests that nutrition and dietary mineral composition may play an important role in cognitive health and the prevention of cognitive disorders (van de Rest et al., 2015). For example, several studies have found associations between adherence to a Mediterranean-style diet, which is rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fish, and healthy fats, and a reduced risk of cognitive decline and dementia (Scarmeas et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2014). Additionally, certain dietary patterns, such as the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) and MIND (Mediterranean-DASH Diet Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) diets, have been specifically designed to target both vascular risk factors and cognitive health (Morris et al., 2015; Sacks et al., 2001).
Dietary mineral composition, including the intake of essential minerals such as calcium, magnesium, potassium, and zinc, may also contribute to cognitive health (Młyniec et al., 2014). Some minerals, such as zinc, play key roles in the modulation of neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity, processes that are critical for learning and memory (Takeda, 2011). Other minerals, such as magnesium, have been implicated in neuronal energy metabolism and the maintenance of neuronal membrane stability (Barbagallo & Dominguez, 2010).
Several studies have examined the relationship between dietary mineral intake and cognitive function. For example, a prospective study by Kesse-Guyot et al. (2011) found that higher dietary magnesium intake was associated with a reduced risk of cognitive decline in older adults. Similarly, a study by Ozawa et al. (2012) observed that higher dietary intake of potassium was associated with a lower risk of dementia in Japanese women.
The role of dietary mineral composition in cognitive health is an area of growing interest, with the potential for the development of dietary interventions and public health strategies aimed at promoting cognitive well-being and preventing cognitive disorders. Further research is needed to elucidate the mechanisms through which dietary minerals may influence cognitive function, as well as to establish optimal intake levels and dietary patterns for cognitive health.

A number of companies, however, have defied this
stereotype of the bumbling corporate behemoth and have
continued to make investments in new ventures. Even as
substantial numbers of corporate venture capitalists have
headed for the exits in the past year and a half, some big
companies – including Intel, Microsoft, and Qualcomm –
have publicly committed themselves to continued high
levels of investment. Others – such as Merck, Lilly, and
Millennium Pharmaceuticals – have actually come in the
door as others have left. What gives these optimists their
confidence? More generally, why have some companies’
forays into venture capital been successful, generating
significant growth for their own businesses?
To answer these questions, we need an orga-
nized way to think about corporate venture capi-
tal, a framework that can help a company decide
whether it should invest in a particular start-up
by first understanding what kind of benefit might
be realized from the investment. This article offers
such a framework, one that also suggests when –
that is, in what kind of economic climates – differ-
ent types of investment are likely to make sense.
But first, let’s briefly define corporate venture
capital. We use the term to describe the invest-
ment of corporate funds directly in external start-up
companies. Our definition excludes investments made
through an external fund managed by a third party, even
if the investment vehicle is funded by and specifically
designed to meet the objectives of a single investing com-
pany. It also excludes investments that fall under the
more general rubric of “corporate venturing” – for exam-
ple, the funding of new internal ventures that, while dis-
tinct from a company’s core business and granted some
organizational autonomy, remain legally part of the com-
pany. Our definition does include, however, investments
made in start-ups that a company has already spun off as
independent businesses.
Our framework helps explain why certain types of cor-
porate VC investments proliferate only when financial
returns are high, why other types persist in good times
and in bad, and why still others make little sense in any
phase of the business cycle. It can also help companies
evaluate their existing and potential VC investments and
determine when and how to use corporate VC as an in-
strument of strategic growth. The Dual Dimensions
of Corporate VC
A corporate VC investment is defined by two characteris-
tics: its objective and the degree to which the operations
of the investing company and the start-up are linked. Al-
though companies typically have a range of objectives for
their VC investments, this type of funding usually ad-
vances one of two fundamental goals. Some investments
are strategic: They are made primarily to increase the
sales and profits of the corporation’s own businesses. A
company making a strategic investment seeks to identify
and exploit synergies between itself and a new venture.
For example, Lucent Venture Partners, which invests the
telecommunications equipment maker’s funds in exter-
nal companies, makes investments in start-ups that are
focused on infrastructure or services for voice or data net-
works. Many of these companies have formal alliances
with Lucent to help sell Lucent’s equipment alongside
their own offerings. While Lucent would clearly like to
make money on its investments in these start-ups, it is
willing to accept low returns if its own businesses perform
better as a result of the investments.
The other investment objective is financial, wherein a
company is mainly looking for attractive returns. Here,
a corporation seeks to do as well as or better than private
VC investors, due to what it sees as its superior knowledge
of markets and technologies, its strong balance sheet, and
its ability to be a patient investor. In addition, a company’s
brand may signal the quality of the start-up to other in-
vestors and potential customers, ultimately returning
rewards to the original investor. For example, Dell Ven-
tures, Dell Computer’s in-house VC operation, has made
numerous Internet investments that it has expected to
earn attractive returns. While the company hopes that
the investments will help its own business grow, the main

summarize this our Ways to Invest
Clearly, neither of these two dimensions of corporate in-
vesting – strategic versus financial and tightly linked
versus loosely linked – is an either-or proposition. Most
investments will fall somewhere along a spectrum be-
tween the two poles of each pair of attributes. Still, over-
laying the two dimensions creates a useful framework
to help a company assess its current and potential VC in-
vestments. (See the exhibit “Mapping Your Corporate VC
Investments” for a depiction of these distinct types of cor-
porate venture capital.)
Driving Investments. This type of investment is char-
acterized by a strategic rationale and tight links between
a start-up and the operations of the investing company.
For instance, Agilent Technologies created a VC operation
to invest in three strategic areas – life sciences, wireless
communications, and optical communications – that it
has identified as key to its growth. The VC arm works
closely with the company’s existing businesses to share
information, qualify investment opportunities, and con-
nect portfolio companies to Agilent’s own initiatives. For
example, Agilent has recently invested in a start-up com-
pany making wireless radio-frequency devices, a product
area Agilent plans to explore in its own business. If this
investment is successful, Agilent’s future business will
benefit; if it fails, Agilent will get a valuable early warning
about pitfalls to avoid in that business.
Similarly, Microsoft has earmarked more than $1 bil-
lion to invest in start-up companies that could help ad-
vance its new Internet services architecture, “.Net.” This
Microsoft technology – which will enable its Windows
platform to provide a variety of Internet services – is a
contender to set the standards for the next generation of
products and services over the Web. Microsoft is funding
start-up firms that will exploit its architecture and, in so
doing, promote the adoption of the Microsoft standard
over rival approaches from Sun Microsystems and IBM.
The start-ups are tightly linked to Microsoft’s operations
through the Windows software and tools that the com-
pany provides to them for the development of their own
products.
The strategic value of Microsoft’s .Net investments is
highlighted by the company’s decision to make them in
the shadow of earlier VC investment losses. The company
has written off staggering sums – $980million in the third
quarter of 2000 alone – in its corporate VC portfolio. But
rather than backing off, Microsoft is charging ahead with
new .Net investments. Because they could help the com-
pany win the battle over the next Internet services stan-
dard – a major strategic victory – it is willing to risk sub-
stantial financial losses.
Although it’s clear that many driving investments can
advance a corporate strategy, there are limits to what they
can achieve. The tight coupling of these investments with
a company’s current processes means that these invest-
ments will sustain the current strategy. They will be un-
likely to help a corporation cope with disruptive strategies
or to identify new opportunities when the company must
go beyond its current capabilities to respond to a change
in the environment. If a corporation wants to transcend
current strategy and processes, it should not rely on driv-
ing investments, which are ill suited for these tasks.
Enabling Investments. In this mode of VC investing,
a company still makes investments primarily for strategic
reasons but does not couple the venture tightly with its
own operations. The theory is that a successful invest-

This may seem too good to be true. How can a company’s
strategy benefit if its operations are not tightly linked
to the venture? One answer lies in the notion of comple-
mentarity: Having one product makes a person want
another. A company can take advantage of this notion by
using its VC investments to stimulate the development of
the ecosystem in which it operates – that is, the suppliers,
customers, and third-party developers that make goods
and services that stimulate demand for the company’s
own offerings.
Intel Capital, the investment arm of the semiconductor
giant, is a paradigmatic example of a company making
enabling investments. Back in the early 1990s, long before
corporate venture capital was fashionable, Intel realized
it could benefit from nurturing start-ups making com-
plementary products: Demand for them could spur in-
creased demand for Intel’s own microprocessor products.
So Intel invested in hundreds of companies whose prod-
ucts – such as video, audio, and graphics hardware and
software – required increasingly powerful microproces-
sors inside the computers they ran on, thereby stimulat-
ing sales of Intel Pentium chips. Whereas Microsoft’s
VC investments in start-ups seek to establish a new stan-
dard, in Intel’s case, the investments have mainly been
aimed at increasing its revenue by boosting sales within
the current Wintel operating system standard.

Chapter 1: The Working Mom's Dilemma

Introduction

Working mothers have been part of society for many years, but their role has evolved significantly over time. Today, the vast majority of women work outside the home, and this has led to a variety of challenges and opportunities. In this chapter, we will explore the history of working mothers, the challenges they face, and the concept of "mom guilt."

A Historical Overview of Working Mothers

In the past, women's roles were limited to domestic duties, and working outside the home was seen as inappropriate for women. However, during World War II, women's labor became critical to the war effort, and more women entered the workforce. After the war, women were expected to return to their domestic duties, but many continued to work outside the home.

In the 1960s and 1970s, the feminist movement helped to increase women's participation in the workforce. The introduction of birth control also gave women greater control over their reproductive choices, allowing them to plan their careers and families.

Today, the majority of women work outside the home, and many are the primary breadwinners for their families. However, despite the progress that has been made, working mothers still face many challenges.

Challenges Faced by Working Moms

Working mothers face a variety of challenges, including:

1. Balancing work and family responsibilities: Many working mothers struggle to balance the demands of their jobs with the needs of their families. This can lead to stress and burnout.
2. Lack of support: Working mothers may not have access to adequate childcare, which can make it difficult to manage work and family responsibilities.
3. Gender bias: Women may face discrimination and bias in the workplace, which can limit their opportunities for advancement.
4. Pay inequality: Women still earn less than men on average, which can make it difficult for working mothers to support their families.
5. Societal expectations: There is often pressure on women to be perfect mothers and perfect employees, which can lead to feelings of guilt and inadequacy.

The Concept of "Mom Guilt"

Many working mothers experience what is known as "mom guilt." This is the feeling of guilt or anxiety that comes from trying to balance work and family responsibilities. Working mothers may feel guilty about not spending enough time with their children, missing important milestones, or not being able to attend school events.

Mom guilt can be overwhelming, and it can make it difficult for working mothers to enjoy their time at work or at home. It is important for working mothers to recognize that they are not alone in their struggles and to seek support when needed.

Conclusion

Working mothers face a variety of challenges, but they also have many opportunities for personal and professional growth. In the following chapters, we will explore the benefits of being a working mom, the impact of gender roles and stereotypes, and how employers can support working mothers. By understanding the challenges and opportunities that working mothers face, we can work together to create a more supportive and inclusive society for all families.

워킹맘의 역사적 개관
과거에는 여성의 역할이 가사 업무에 국한되었고 집 밖에서 일하는 것은 여성에게 적합하지 않은 것으로 여겨졌습니다. 그러나 제2차 세계 대전 중에 여성의 노동력이 전쟁 노력에 결정적인 역할을 하게 되었고 더 많은 여성이 노동력에 투입되었습니다. 전쟁이 끝난 후 여성들은 가사 업무로 돌아가야 했지만 많은 여성들이 계속해서 집 밖에서 일했습니다.

오늘날 대부분의 여성은 집 밖에서 일하며 많은 여성이 가족을 부양해야 합니다. 그러나 이러한 진전에도 불구하고 워킹맘들은 여전히 ​​많은 어려움에 직면해 있습니다.
워킹맘이 직면한 도전
워킹맘은 다음과 같은 다양한 문제에 직면합니다.
1. 일과 가족에 대한 책임의 균형: 많은 워킹맘들은 직업과 가족의 필요 사이에서 균형을 맞추는 데 어려움을 겪습니다. 이것은 스트레스와 소진으로 이어질 수 있습니다.

3. 성별 편견: 여성은 직장에서 차별과 편견에 직면할 수 있으며, 이로 인해 승진 기회가 제한될 수 있습니다.

5. 사회적 기대: 종종 여성에게 완벽한 어머니와 완벽한 직원이 되어야 한다는 압력이 있으며, 이는 죄책감과 부적절함을 유발할 수 있습니다.
"엄마 죄책감"의 개념
많은 일하는 어머니들은 "엄마 죄책감"으로 알려진 것을 경험합니다. 이것은 일과 가족 책임의 균형을 맞추려고 노력하는 데서 오는 죄책감이나 불안감입니다. 일하는 어머니는 자녀와 충분한 시간을 보내지 않거나 중요한 이정표를 놓치거나 학교 행사에 참석할 수 없는 것에 대해 죄책감을 느낄 수 있습니다.

결론
일하는 어머니는 다양한 도전에 직면하지만 개인적 및 직업적 성장을 위한 많은 기회도 있습니다. 다음 장에서는 워킹맘의 이점, 성역할과 고정관념의 영향, 고용주가 워킹맘을 지원할 수 있는 방법에 대해 알아볼 것입니다. 워킹맘이 직면한 도전과 기회를 이해함으로써 우리는 모든 가족을 위해 보다 지원적이고 포용적인 사회를 만들기 위해 함께 노력할 수 있습니다.

fait le poster de mon projet tut sachant que c'est un jeu d'avion en realité virtuel en suivant les regles suivante:
La construction du poster de présentation du PTUT

La forme
• Un format standard A0 (84,1 cm \* 118,9 cm).
• Une orientation paysage ou portrait
• Une taille de polices normée : 
o 59 à 64 pts pour le titre du poster
o 38 à 42 pts pour les noms d'auteurs et l'adresse des auteurs
o environ 40 pts pour les titres niveau 1
o 24 pts minimum pour le corps du texte
• Une marge de 2,5 cm sur tout le pourtour du poster
• Règle de composition : 30 % texte, 30 % blanc, 40 % de figures graphiques
• Veiller au contraste : si le fond est foncé, utiliser une police d’écriture claire et inversement
• Harmoniser l’ensemble (couleur, forme, police)

Le contenu
• Le titre
• Le nom des auteurs, leur affiliation, le sigle de l'université, la date
• L’introduction : le contexte / l'objectif présenté de manière synthétique
• le matériel et les méthodes (le nombre de personnes, la qualification ou les compétences, les outils, les innovations, les étapes dans la gestion du projet)
• Les résultats mis en valeur
• La conclusion (les applications et les perspectives)
• Les remerciements et les logos avec la mention des partenaires 
• Le ou les contacts
• Les sources / les partenaires le cas échéant
• Rédiger des phrases courtes.
• Son contenu doit être facilement accessible même pour un lecteur autonome. Il est donc nécessaire d’adopter une stratégie de communication attractive, structurée et concise.
Le titre
Le titre doit interpeler, informer et annoncer.
Il peut :
• Être direct 
Ex : Chat GPT, les nouveaux enjeux de l’intelligence artificielle
• Exposer un conflit
Ex : Intelligence artificielle : cauchemar ou révolution ?
• Poser une question 
Ex : Incidence et risque des nouveaux usages de l'intelligence artificielle - de quoi Chat GPT est-il le nom ?
• Présenter un jeu de mots 
Ex : Donner sa langue au Chat GPT
Un bon titre, c’est quoi ?
• Facile à mémoriser
• Valable pour un seul poster
• Ne heurte pas le lecteur
Le contenu textuel
• Les effets artistiques ne remplacent pas un bon contenu
• Les informations partagées doivent être pertinentes et précises.
• L’introduction est le fil conducteur. Elle est composée d’environ 25 mots définissant le comment, le pourquoi, et le message principal du poster. Chaque partie du poster doit se rattacher au fil conducteur
• Les parties « méthodes et résultats » doivent représenter les 2/3 du poster
• Faire preuve d’esprit de synthèse : le volume de texte n’excède pas 1/3 de la surface
• Utiliser des phrases courtes
• Privilégier la forme impersonnelle et la voie passive
• Omettre les informations inutiles

Les figures graphiques
Elles doivent pouvoir à elles seules transmettre un message. 
La figure graphique ne doit pas être une illustration mais une contribution à la compréhension
Pour cela, on veille à leur qualité :
• Valeur informative / pertinence
• Clarté des données
• Disponibilité / droits d’auteur
• Résolution entre 300 et 600 dpi pour du A0 (dpi = point par pouce)
Il faut les retravailler pour :
• Améliorer leur impact
• Éliminer le surplus d’information
• Mettre en valeur les chiffres significatifs
• Insérer des légendes
Les images qui retiennent le plus l'attention du lecteur sont : 
Photo > Dessin > Schéma > Tableau


Étapes de construction

Étape 0 - Se répartir les tâches au sein du groupe
Étape 1 - Connaitre sa cible et définir le fil conducteur
- Décider du focus par lequel attirer l’attention. Règle des 3 secondes pour inciter le lecteur à conserver son intérêt 30 secondes supplémentaires.
- Déterminer à quel niveau d’information je souhaite faire parvenir ma cible, quel niveau de détail et de précision je dois donner.
- Il faut identifier le message principal du poster. Ce sera le fil conducteur qu’il faudra garder à l’esprit tout au long de la préparation. Chaque partie du poster doit s’y rattacher.
Étape 2 - Trier et organiser l’information au brouillon
- Passer par un format papier pour agencer au brouillon l’information (titre, bloc de textes, procédés graphiques)
- Choisir le sens du poster (portrait ou paysage)
- Définir le sens de lecture, naturel ou explicite, du poster
- Définir une mise en page intelligente (qui a du sens) et originale.
o Exemples :
 Un cercle pour la résolution d’un problème
Un arbre qui porte ses fruits pour illustrer la réorganisation réussie d’un service, d’une entreprise…
Un jeu de l’oie pour montrer les étapes du projet
- Bien mettre en évidence le point de départ s’il n’est pas situé en haut à gauche (graphisme, couleur…)
Étape 3 - Produire le contenu des différents blocs
- Chaque cadre développe une idée précise en relation avec le sujet.
- Rédiger les titres, sous titres
- Placer les mots clefs

## Bölüm Özeti

\* Hocanın konu anlatımı burada \*
Sosyolojiye giriş dersine hoş geldiniz. Bu ilk dersimizde sizlerle, kısaca bilim olarak sosyoloji, sosyolojinin temel kavramları ve sosyoloji diğer sosyal bilimleri ilişkiler üzerinde duracağız. Hiç merak ettiniz mi günümüzün gençliğiyle onların anne babalarının değerleri arasındaki farkları ya da şunlar hakkında hiç düşündünüz mü? Neden günümüzdeki aile yapısı geçmişten farklıdır veya toplumda neden kadınlar ikinci plandadır, geri plandadır veya birçok toplumda boşanmalar giderek artıyor, bizde de artıyor. Neden boşanmalar artıyor veya aşk evlilikleri geliniksel toplumlarda neden yaygın değildi? Bu ve buna benzer her gün yüzlerce soru soruyoruz. Aslında bu sorular sormaya başladığınızda amatör sosyoloji yapmaya başladığınız demektir. Sosyoloji latince birliktelik anlamına gelen socuyu sözcüyle, Yunanca İnceleme Stadi ya da çalışma anlamına gelen logos sözcüklerinin bir araya getirilmesinden oluşmaktadır. Kelime anlamıyla sosyoloji toplumsal üyeliğin temellerinin incelenmesini ifade etmektedir. Sosyolojinin isim babası Ogus Comptdur ve sosyoloji için ilk kullandığı sözcük, ilk ürettiği sözcük sosyal fiziktir. Daha sonra Compt sosyal fizik ifadesini kavramına terk etmiş onun yerine sosyoloji sözcüğünü ifade etmiştir. Sosyolojinin çok farklı tanımları var. Ortak noktaları da var elbette bu tanımların. Dür kayma göre sosyoloji toplumsal kurumları incelenen bilim dalıdır. Bir başka sosyoloji göre toplumsal fenomenleri ve bere göre toplumsal eylemi simese göre insan ilişkilerini incelenen bilim dalıdır. En genel tanımlarından birisi sosyolojinin insan toplumunun sistematik ve belli bir kuşku ve belli bir metod içerisinde incelenmesini ifade etmektedir. Bir sosyoluk günümüzde güreşin altındaki her şeyin sosyolojisi olduğunu söylüyor. Yani bugün artık iktisadın sosyolojisi var, siyasetin sosyolojisi var, hukukun sosyolojisi var. Aklınıza gelecek kültürün vesaire aşkın her şeyin sosyolojisi var. İki insan bir araya geldiği zaman orada bir toplumsal ilişki başlıyor ve 10 noktadan sonra bir takım sosyolojik analizleri yapmanız mümkün hale geliyor. Bir sosyoloj diyor ki sosyoloji bize içinde yaşadığımız topluma uzaylı yaratıklar gibi bakma becerisi kazandırır. İlk anda bu sinir bozucu bir sözcük olarak gelebilir size. Ama biz içinde yaşadığımız toplumun dışına çıkmadığımız müddetçe bazı şeyleri kavramamız zorlaşmaktadır. Çünkü sürekli aynı toplumun içinde yaşayan insanlar bir süre sonra o yaşadıkları deneyimlere alışmakta ve onun üzerine düşünmemektedirler. Dolayısıyla bir anlamda sosyoloji alışık olduğumuz perspektifin dışına çıkmaktadır. Dolayısıyla bunun bir rahatsız hepçisi edici tarafı da söz konusudur. Dolayısıyla sosyolojik perspektif bir dünyaya farklı bakış açısı sunmaktadır. Ve tabii farklı dünyalar arasında sosyoloji yeni pencereler açmaktadır. Bir diğer ifadeyle sosyoloji içinde yaşadığımız dünyayı daha geniş bir bağlamda görme imkanı sağlamaktadır. Kemen sorularından bir tanesi insanların toplum tarafından nasıl etkilendiydir? Bir diğer ifadeyle sosyolojik hayal gücü içinde yaşadığımız toplum ve kendimiz arasındaki ilişkiyi görme imkanı sağlar. Eğer biz içinde yaşadığımız toplumu iyi anlayamazsak aslında kendimizi anlamamız da çok kolay değildir. Çünkü biz insanlar bir taraftan toplumu toplumsal ilişkileri biçimlendirirken diğer taraftan toplumsal toplum ve toplumlu toplumsal ilişkiler tarafından biçimlendirilen varlıklarız. Rite-Messi söylediği gibi sosyoloji tarih ile biyografi arasındaki ilişkiyi daha iyi kavramamıza yardımcı oluyor. Ve bizler açısından toplumun ve içinde yaşadığımız tarihsel süreçlerin bir ürünü olduğumuzu fark etmemizi sağlıyor. Biz toplumu ve birey birlikte anlamadıkça ne bireyin hayatını ne de tarihi tam olarak kavramamız söz konusu değildiyor. Dur kayma göre toplum bireylerin basit bir toplamı değildir. Onun için toplum kendine has nitelikleri olan özgül bir gerçekliği temsil etmektedir. Tabi belki toplumu bir cümle ile tanımlamak gerekebilir. O da şu anlama geliyor toplum dediğimiz şey burada bir kültür ve bölgeyi paylaşan insan grubunu kastediyoruz. Bir başka tanımda da toplumu ortak kültürü paylaşan belli bir toplak toprak parçası üzerinde yerleşik, kendilerini birleşik ve özgün varlık olarak gören insanlardan oluşan bir grup olarak tanımlamak mümkündür. Sosyoloji'nin kuşkusuz en önemli isimlerinden birisi kurcubabalarından birisi de Max Weber'dır. Weber'e göre sosyoloji toplumsal davranışı ya da toplumsal eğlemi inceleyen bilim dalının adıdır. Weber toplumsal eğlemi dört grupta sınıflıyor. Bunlardan birincisi amaçla ilgili toplumsal eğlen, diğeri değerle ilişkili toplumsal eğlen, bir başkası duygusal eğlen ya da duygusal davranış son olarak da geleneksel davranış şeklinde bir sınıflanmaya tabi tutuyor. Weber amaçla ilgili rasyonel davranışı anlatırken şunu kastediyor. Diyor ki insanların belli amaçları var. Bu amaçlara ulaşabilmek için belli hesap kitaplar yaparlar. Bu çerçevede kendileri için en az maliyetle, en kazançlı olanı gerçekleştirmeye çalışırlar. Bu konuda verdiği örneklerden birisi amacı yönelik rasyonel davranışa ilişkin verdiği örneklerden birisi köprü yapan mühendisin davranışıdır. İkinci davranış biçimi, değeri ilişkin rasyonel davranışı idi. Burada da belli bir rasyonellik var ama bu amacı yönelik rasyonel davranıştan farklıdır. Örneğin gemisiyle batan kaptanın davranışı aslında değeri yönelik rasyonel davranıştır. Yani görülür de kaptanın kendisiyle kurtarması lazım fakat orada bir kaptanın en önemli değerlerinden birisi, gemiyi kaptanın terk etmeyeceği ise, gemisiyle sahip çıkması gerektiği ise bu bir tür değerden kaynaklanan rasyonelteyi ifade eder. Duygusal davranış dediğimiz şey rasyonel davranışın aslında biraz karşısındaki bir davranış biçimi. Rasyonel davranış hesaplı, kitaplı, kontrolülü amaç odaklı bir davranış olmasına karşılık. Duygusal davranış sonuçlarını hesap etmeden kişinin duygularına kapılarak yaptığı davranışa duygusal davranış diyoruz. Örneğin alayın çocuğa tokat vuran annenin davranışını düşündüğünüzde aslında bu bir tür duygusal davranış olarak ifade edebileceğimiz davranış biçimidir. Çünkü alayan çocuğa siz tokat vuruyorsanız bu çocuğun susması mümkün değildir, daha çok ağlayacaktır. Ama orada arnaya artık bunu almıştır ve dolayısıyla ister istemez duygularına kapılıp böyle bir tepki gösterebilir. Gelimeksel davranış ise içinde yaşadığımız geleneklerin bize zorladığı davranış biçimidir. Yani yüzlerce yıldır insanlar belli toprağı belli şekillerde ekip biçiyorlardır, belli şekillerde ilişki kuruyorlardır. Birbirlerine karşı baba oğul da oğul babaya ya da anne çocuğa, çocuk anneye karşı ya da büyüklerle küçükler arasında belli ilişki biçimi vardır. Bu ilişki biçimi yüzlerce yıldır artık alışkanlık ve gelene kalene gelmiştir ve bizim davranışlarımızın temel kaynağı burada artık o yüzlerce yıldır süren gelenektir. Bu birey ve toplum konusu sosyal ve biçok alanda çok tartışılan konulardan birisidir. Bir zamanlar İngiltere'nin başbakanlığını yapan Margaret Thatcher'ın bir sözü vardı, çok tartışılan şöyle diyordu Thatcher, toplum diye bir şey yoktur diyordu, sadece bireyler kadınlar ve erkekler vardır. Gerçekten de Thatcher'ın dediği gibi toplum diye bir şey yok mu, sadece kadınlar ve erkekler mi var, eğer toplum diye bir şey yoksa o zaman sosyolojiye ne gerek var? Bu elbette sosyolojik perspektif içerisinde kabul edilebilecek bir söz değil. Sosyolojik hayal gücünü açıklarken Wright Bills şunu söylüyor, bizim diyor bireysel gibi gördüğümüz bir çok sorunun aslında toplumsal bir temeli vardır. Örneğin işlerimizi iyi gittiği zamanlarda hepimiz kendi başarılarımıza çok fırgı yaparız. Sürekli övünürüz, şunları başardık, bunları gerçekleştirdik vesaire diye. Ve bunları hep sorarlarsa kendimizin yaptığını söyleriz. Bunları bizim başarımız olarak sunarız. Ama gün gelir büyük bir ekonomik kriz ortaya çıkar, kazançlarımızın hepsi yok olur gider. Sonra anlarız ki hepimiz aslında toplumun bize sunduğu imkanlar kadar belli şeyleri başarabiliyoruz. Eğer içinde yaşadığımız toplum bize şu anda kişisel olarak bireysel çabamızda başardığımızı söylediğimiz şeyleri, imkanları sunmamış olsalardı çok muhtemeldir ki bizler şu anda bunları başaramamış olurduk. Dolayısıyla eğer toplumu anlayamazsanız bireysel davranışı da anlamanız tam anlamıyla mümkün değildir. Peki, sosyoloji bize ne kazandırır? Neden dünyanın dört bir yanında neresine giderseniz giden dünyanın, sosyoloji diye bir bilimin olduğunu görürsünüz, üniversitelerde okutulduğunu görürsünüz. Sadece sosyolojinin, sosyoloji bölümlerinde değil, bütün sosyal bilimler bölümlerinde sosyoloji ya da bazıları dersleri görebilirsiniz. Neden dünyada milyarlarca insan böyle bir eğitim için ihtiyaç duyuyor, böyle bir ders için ihtiyaç duyuyor? Ne kazandırıyor sosyoloji bize? Aslında iyi bir sosyoloji eğitimi almış birey, toplumsal hayat hakkındaleştirile düşünmeye öğrenir, sorgulamayı öğrenir. Sosyolojik hayal gücü bize gündelik hayatın ötesine geçme imkanı sağlar. Yine toplumsal ilişkileri bir sakkında sosyoloji farkındalığımızı artırır. Bağımana göre iyi bir sosyoloji eğitimi duygularımızı keskinleştirip gözlerimizin daha çok açılmasına yardımcı olur. Daha önce görmediğimiz insanlık hallerini görme imkanı sağlar. Bir diğer ifadeyle sosyoloji ya da iyi bir sosyoloji eğitimi baskıcı dünyayı esnekleştirir. Bize dünyanın şimdikinden daha farklı olabileceğini gösterir. Dolayısıyla iyi bir sosyoloji eğitimi almış birey'i manifel edebilmek çok kolay değildir. Sosyoloji insanların empatiye tekniklerini, ötekini daha iyi anlama becerilerini artırır. Korku ve zıplaşma yerine iyi bir sosyoloji eğitimi hoşgörüyü teşvik eder. İnsanların özgürlüğüne katkı da bulunur. Bu sebeple sosyoloji sık sık bazı toplumlarda politik ihanetle de suçlanabilir. Kont tahmin etmek için bilmek, kontrol etmek için tahmin etmek gibi bir söz söylüyor. Diyor ki, bir anlamda biz bazı şeyleri kontrol edebilmek için doğru tahmin edilmemiz gerekiyor. Dolayısıyla biz içinde yaşadığımız toplumun oyunun kurallarını ne kadar iyi bilirsek o toplumda oyunu o kadar iyi anlayabiliriz. Bazı konularda ne kadar sağlıklı bilgimiz varsa, gelecekte o sorunları çözmeye yönelik o derece yüksek becerilerimiz olabilir. Kısaca sosyoloji ve diğer sosyal bilimler ilişkiler üzerinde duracağız bu bölümde. Biliyorsunuz sosyal bilimlerden birisi, tek bir sosyal bilim danı sosyal değil. Örneğin, satsak bir sosyal bilim danıdır, siyaset bir sosyal bilim danıdır, psikoloji bir sosyal bilim danıdır. Peki bunların arasındaki farklar neler? Örneğin psikoloji bireysel farklara özellikle zekâ ve kişilik gibi konuları odaklanıyor. İlgilendiği konular arasında biriyin algılama, öğrenme gülüleri, bellek gibi süreçler söz konusu. Dolayısıyla, ikisi de sosyal bilim olmasına rağmen bu iki bir bilimin odak noktaları birbirinden farklıdır. Benzer şekilde, etsat bilimine baktığımız zaman etsat, kıt kaynaklarla maksimum üretimi gerçekleştirmeyi amaçlayan bir bilim olarak ifade ediliyor. Odak noktasında malların ve hizmetlerin üretim, tüketim, dağıtımı gibi konular var. Sosyoloji de belli ölçüde bu konularla ilgileniyor fakat amaçları birbirinden farklı. Sosyoloji ekonomik, etsat bilimi arasındaki temel fark odaklandıkları temel noktalardır. Sosyoloji doğrudan toplumsalın kendine odaklanıyor, toplumsal ilişkiyi odaklanıyor, kurumlara odaklanıyor. Etsat ise üretim, tüketim gibi birtakım süreçlere odaklanıyor. Dolayısıyla psikoloji de olduğu gibi, etsatla sosyoloji arasındaki temel fark da bu odak noktası farkı. The Next.js router uses server-centric routing with client-side navigation. It supports instant loading states and concurrent rendering. This means navigation maintains client-side state, avoids expensive re-renders, is interruptible, and doesn't cause race conditions.

There are two ways to navigate between routes:

 Component
useRouter Hook
This page will go through how to use , useRouter(), and dive deeper into how navigation works.

Usage
To use , import it from next/link, and pass a href prop to the component:

}
There are optional props you can pass to . See the API reference for more information.

Example: Linking to Dynamic Segments
When linking to dynamic segments, you can use template literals and interpolation to generate a list of links. For example, to generate a list of blog posts:

useRouter() Hook
The useRouter hook allows you to programmatically change routes inside Client Components.

To use useRouter, import it from next/navigation, and call the hook inside your Client Component:

'use client';

import { useRouter } from 'next/navigation';

export default function Page() {
 const router = useRouter();

 );
